passage: In the textile factory's HR office, Vandana, twenty-two, sat across from Nitin, the HR officer. She'd been offered a job at a rival factory with better pay, but her contract required thirty days' notice. "They want me to start Monday," she said. "My mother's rent is due, and my brother's college fees." Nitin nodded. "Legally, you owe us the notice period. But I understand." Vandana looked at her hands. She could just stop coming. Some people did. But she had signed. "I'll serve the notice," she said. "Can I ask them to wait?" She called the new factory from the office phone, explained, and they agreed to three weeks. That evening, she sent her mother money from her savings for the rent and voted in the union election on her way home.

qa.q: How many days' notice did Vandana's contract require?
qa.a: Thirty days.

qa.q: What was Vandana tempted to do, and why did she decide against it?
qa.a: She was tempted to simply stop coming, but she felt bound by the contract she had signed and determined to act honourably.

qa.q: What made her choice of calling the new factory smart?
qa.a: It kept her promise to the old employer while protecting the new job, showing both sides respect.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Vandana's decision?
qa.a: Nitin is probably relieved and respects her for honouring the contract even under money pressure.

grounding: Shows a young worker honouring a workplace contract while supporting her family and taking part in civic life.

passage:
Dear Gurleen,

It's been six months in this city and I finally feel like I'm managing, mostly.

I pay my own rent now, on the first of every month, before I buy anything else. I send some money home every month too. Amma keeps saying I shouldn't, but Appa's shop is slow and I can tell she worries. I sort their bills on my phone when I call on Sundays.

Last week, I went to my first resident welfare meeting in our building. They were deciding about the broken water pump. I was the youngest there and nervous, but I spoke up about the leaking pipes too. They added it to the list!

It's a lot. Some nights I'm exhausted. But I like knowing people can count on me.

Love,
Keerthana

qa.q: When does Keerthana pay her rent?
qa.a: On the first of every month, before buying anything else.

qa.q: What does Keerthana mean when she says she likes knowing people can count on her?
qa.a: She feels proud and grounded taking responsibility for herself, her parents and her community, even when it's tiring.

qa.q: What would you advise Keerthana so she doesn't burn out?
qa.a: Keep some rest time for herself each week and let her parents share their worries so she's not carrying everything silently.

qa.q: How might Amma feel about the money Keerthana sends?
qa.a: She may feel guilty accepting it and worried about her daughter, but also grateful and proud.

grounding: A young woman writes about handling her own finances, supporting her parents and joining local civic decisions.

passage: Pranav rubbed his eyes and laughed. "Rukmini, you asked what adulting actually looks like? Okay. Mine is Tuesday nights. That's when I sit at the dining table with a folder: my rent, Papa's electricity bill, Ma's medicine refills, my salary slip. Papa retired last year and he's still figuring out the online payments, so I do them with him slowly, so he can learn. Then on the first Sunday of the month, I go to the residents' association meeting. At first I went just because Papa asked. Now I actually care. Last month we got the street light fixed near the bus stop where girls wait at night. Nobody tells you it's this boring and this important at the same time. I complain, but I'd feel strange not doing it."

qa.q: What does Pranav do on Tuesday nights?
qa.a: He sits at the dining table with a folder of bills, rent and his salary slip.

qa.q: How does Pranav feel about these duties?
qa.a: He finds them boring but also important, and he'd feel strange not doing them, which shows he has made them his own.

qa.q: What was wise about Pranav doing payments slowly with his father?
qa.a: It helps his father learn and keep some independence, instead of Pranav simply taking over.

qa.q: How might the girls waiting at the bus stop be affected by the association's work?
qa.a: The fixed street light makes them safer at night, even though they may never know who pushed for it.

grounding: A young man describes managing household bills, supporting his retired parents and taking part in community decisions.

passage: I'm Maria, and I sit across from Jagdish at the accounts office. He's twenty-two and the most regular person I know. Every first of the month, before lunch, he sends part of his salary home to his parents in Nashik, and I've heard him on the phone asking about his father's physiotherapy. Last month the firm asked everyone to work the election weekend; our contracts say that overtime is voluntary. Jagdish said he couldn't, because he had signed up as a polling volunteer, and he showed the manager the letter. He offered to come in early the Monday after instead, and he did, at seven. I don't know if he ever gets tired of being responsible. He did fall asleep at his desk once, briefly, and was embarrassed when I teased him.

qa.q: Where do Jagdish's parents live?
qa.a: In Nashik.

qa.q: Why might Jagdish have been embarrassed when Maria teased him?
qa.a: He takes his duties seriously and may have felt that dozing at work didn't fit his idea of being responsible.

qa.q: How could Jagdish's manager support someone like him?
qa.a: By respecting the voluntary overtime terms and his civic commitments, and noticing if he is overstretched.

qa.q: How does Maria seem to feel about Jagdish?
qa.a: Maria respects and slightly marvels at his reliability, and teases him warmly.

grounding: Shows a young adult supporting his parents, keeping to his work contract and volunteering at elections, seen by a colleague.

passage:
October: Imran, twenty-one, signed his first job contract at the logistics firm and read every clause twice, including the notice period. Two weeks later his father's knee surgery was scheduled. That night he sat on the hospital bench with his friend Manoj, doing sums: rent, Abba's medicines, his own bus fare.
November: He rearranged everything. Early shifts, so he could take Abba to physiotherapy in the evenings. Electricity and rent paid on the first. He still found an hour on Sunday to help Manoj's residents' group repaint the zebra crossing near the school.
December: Abba walked to the mosque without a stick. Imran slept till ten for the first time in weeks, and nobody woke him.

qa.q: What did Imran help repaint in November?
qa.a: The zebra crossing near the school.

qa.q: What does Imran reading every clause twice suggest about his attitude?
qa.a: It suggests he took his first job seriously and felt cautious, wanting to understand every obligation before relying on it.

qa.q: How did Imran manage so many duties at once?
qa.a: He planned: early shifts to free his evenings, bills paid first, and a small fixed time for community work.

qa.q: How might Abba have felt watching Imran over these months?
qa.a: Grateful and perhaps a little guilty for needing help, and proud of his son's steadiness.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult meeting job, household, parental-care and community obligations over three months.
